title: Where Is It?
description: Ask where anything is, say here, there, in, on and next to, and name the places you go every week: the souq, the mosque, the school, the hospital, the bathroom and the kitchen. Plus فيه — the one word that says 'there is'.
approach: A neighbourhood map and a house plan: places light up as they are named; location words are learned by moving a key around the plan; وين and فيه are produced from the first minute.
unlock_condition: ≥11/14 on the map tap quiz and a recorded وين question with its answer
can_do: Say here, there, in, on and next to
Name the places you go every week

grammar.title: وين؟ — where, with the thing or the person stuck on
grammar.explanation: وين is the whole question: وين السوق؟ where is the souq, وين المفتاح؟ where is the key. To ask where a person is, stick the ending you know onto وين: وينك؟ where are you, وينه؟ where is he, وينها؟ where is she. From where is من وين, and to where is لوين. The answer is a place with في or بـ in front of it. The MSA أين is never said.

examples.english: Where are you? — I'm at the souq
Where is your mother? — In the kitchen

grammar.title: فيه / ما فيه — there is, there isn't, and where
grammar.explanation: فيه (literally 'in it') means 'there is / there are': فيه قهوة؟ is there coffee. Put ما in front for 'there isn't': ما فيه ماي. After it you can add where, using في or its short twin بـ (both mean in/at — بالبيت and في البيت are the same), على for on, and جنب for next to. Kuwaitis also say أكو / ماكو and Emiratis هست / ما هست; recognise them, but فيه works everywhere.

examples.english: There is a mosque next to the house
Is there water in the fridge? — Yes there is

examples.arabic: الكتاب على الكرسي، مو على الطاولة
examples.transliteration: il-kitaab ʿala l-kursi, mu ʿala ṭ-ṭaawla
examples.english: The book is on the chair, not on the table

culture.title: Ask a stranger — it's expected
culture.note: Nobody in the Gulf expects you to find your way alone; asking a passer-by, a shopkeeper or a guard is normal and often ends with them walking you there. Open with لو سمحت يا أخوي (or يا أختي to a woman) and ask وين + the place. Landmarks are mosques, roundabouts and big shops rather than street names — 'next to the mosque' is a real address. Thank the helper with يعطيك العافية.

phrases.english: Excuse me, where is the mosque?

culture.title: Where you can walk in
culture.note: A mosque welcomes anyone to look from the door, and many large ones (Sheikh Zayed in Abu Dhabi, the Grand Mosque in Kuwait) run visitor tours; shoes come off at the entrance and prayer times are not visiting times. A shop, a café and a mall are open to all. A private majlis you enter only when invited — and then حياك الله means the door is truly open. Bathrooms are usually signed حمام or دورة المياه; ask for either.

phrases.english: The bathroom is here, on the right

vocabulary.teaching_note: Said wayn everywhere in the Gulf; the MSA أين and the Egyptian فين are never used. Takes suffixes like a noun: وينك؟ وينه؟ وينهم؟. You met it in وين تلفوني؟ back in Lesson 1.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man on a street corner with a phone in hand, looking around with a questioning face.
vocabulary.video_hint: Someone searching for keys or a phone; asking a passer-by for directions; وينك on the phone.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The Kuwait–Bahrain–Qatar–Emirates form; Saudis say هنا, and both are used everywhere. تعال هني — come here. Also هنيه in Bahrain and the Emirates.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand pointing straight down at the ground at the speaker's feet.
vocabulary.video_hint: تعال هني to a child or friend; pointing at the spot where something is.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Said hnaak, with the first vowel almost gone. Pair it with ذاك from Lesson 8: ذاك البيت هناك. Kuwaitis also say غاد for over there.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand pointing into the distance at a building across an open square.
vocabulary.video_hint: Pointing across a distance in tour or directions clips.

vocabulary.teaching_note: In or at. Gulf speakers use the short twin بـ just as often — في البيت and بالبيت are the same. Do not confuse في with فيه (there is): the h at the end changes the meaning.
vocabulary.image_scene: A key inside a glass bowl, seen from the side, on a table.
vocabulary.video_hint: Any location statement — في البيت, بالسوق — in vlogs.

vocabulary.teaching_note: On top of. Often shortened to ع in speech: عالطاولة for على الطاولة. You met it in على الكرسي (Lesson 1) and على خير (Lesson 2).
vocabulary.image_scene: A book lying on top of a chair seat, seen from slightly above.

example.english: The phone is on the chair

vocabulary.video_hint: Something placed on a table or shelf and named.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Said jamb — the n turns into m before the b. Kuwait and the Emirates also say يم yamm. This is the word that makes a mosque an address: جنب المسجد.
vocabulary.image_scene: A small coffee cup placed right beside a dallah on a tray.

example.english: The house is next to the mosque

vocabulary.video_hint: Directions given with landmarks; something set down beside another thing.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Gulf g: suug. The traditional market and, loosely, any shopping — رحت السوق can mean the mall. Plural أسواق. It is on the always-allowed list because it appears in half the dialogues you will ever hear.
vocabulary.image_scene: A covered souq alley with spice sacks and lanterns, shoppers in thobes and abayas.

example.english: My mother is at the souq

vocabulary.video_hint: Souq and mall vlogs; رحت السوق in daily narration.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Said masjid, or مسيد masyid up the Gulf. A big Friday mosque is a جامع. The most reliable landmark in any neighbourhood.
vocabulary.image_scene: A white mosque with a single minaret and a dome against a blue sky.

example.english: The mosque is close to the house

vocabulary.video_hint: Neighbourhood tours; the call to prayer with the mosque on screen.

vocabulary.teaching_note: A she-word (ends in ة), so it takes هذي and feminine adjectives: مدرسة كبيرة. Plural مدارس. Stress the middle syllable: mad-RA-sa.
vocabulary.image_scene: A school building with a courtyard and a flag, children in uniform at the gate.
vocabulary.video_hint: School-run mornings in family vlogs; back-to-school shopping.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Four syllables: mus-TASH-fa. The word you need in an emergency, so say it until it is automatic. Emiratis may also say الصحية for a clinic.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hospital entrance with a red crescent sign and an ambulance outside.
vocabulary.video_hint: Anyone heading to hospital in a vlog; hospital signage on screen.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Ends in ع. A big road is طريق. Streets are named after people and numbers, but locals give directions by landmark, not street name.
vocabulary.image_scene: A wide sunny street lined with palms and white villas, a white SUV driving past.

example.english: The car is in the street

vocabulary.video_hint: Driving vlogs; children playing in the street.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Doubled m and the deep ح. The polite public sign is دورة المياه; تواليت is also understood. The single most-asked وين question for a visitor.
vocabulary.image_scene: A bathroom door with a simple pictogram sign, slightly ajar.

example.english: The bathroom is next to the kitchen

vocabulary.video_hint: House tours; asking for the bathroom in a restaurant.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Emphatic ط then خ — two of the throat-and-tongue sounds in one word. Where the vlogs happen: cooking channels start with أنا بالمطبخ.
vocabulary.image_scene: A bright kitchen with a pot on the stove and a tray of tea glasses on the counter.

example.english: My grandmother is in the kitchen

vocabulary.video_hint: Cooking channels; house tours reaching the kitchen.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Not a verb, just a word that says something exists: فيه قهوة؟ Answer إي فيه. Kuwait's أكو and the Emirates' هست mean the same; you will hear them, and فيه is understood by both. The negative ما فيه comes in Lesson 11.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand lifting the lid of a dallah to show coffee inside, steam rising.

example.english: There is tea in the kitchen

vocabulary.video_hint: Checking a fridge or a pot; فيه ماي؟ at a table.

dialogue.transliteration: law samaḥt ya akhuuy, wayn is-suug?
dialogue.english: Excuse me brother, where is the souq?

dialogue.speaker: Passer-by

sound_spotlight.explanation: Two long vowels side by side in this lesson: the ay of وين and the uu of سوق. Gulf holds them long; clipping them (wen, sug) makes the words hard to catch. Stretch them on purpose.
The souq keeps its Gulf g, and because the vowel before it is long and dark, the g is soft at the end — almost a sigh. Compare with the g at the start of قهوة.
The same split, now in place words. Saudis say masjid and jamb; Kuwaitis and Emiratis often say masyid and yamm. Same mosque, same spot beside it.

lesson_sequence.detail: A neighbourhood map: mosque, souq, school, hospital, a street, a house. One line of English: today you ask where things are. Tap يلّا.
Seven place cards; each lights its building on the map as it plays. Then the house plan: kitchen and bathroom. Tap to replay.
A key is dragged around the house plan; the app says على الكرسي, في المطبخ, جنب الباب. Then audio plays and the learner drops the key where it belongs.
An object from Lesson 1 disappears; the learner records وين + the object; the native answers with a location; the learner taps it on the plan.
Six fridge / room scenes: the learner records فيه + item when it is there, taps ما فيه when it is not (heard only, built in Lesson 11).
The directions dialogue plays with the map animating; second pass the learner takes Sara's lines.
Fourteen items mixing place tap, location drop and وين questions. Counter rolls to 120. Nudge: ask one وين question this week.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Walk through your home and say where three things are: التلفون على الطاولة، المفتاح بالمطبخ…
Next time you are out, ask someone وين + a place — even a bathroom in a café. Listen for هناك and جنب in the answer.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Hide an object and let your tutor ask وين؟ Answer with في / على / جنب. Then swap.
